chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Salih ibn al-Sindi, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Three [actions] are responded to with the plural response, even if the person is alone: when one sneezes, it is said, 'May Allah have mercy on you all,' even if there is no one else with him; and when a man greets another man, saying, 'Peace be upon you all,' and when a man supplicates for another man, saying, 'May Allah grant you well-being,' even if he is alone, for there are others [angels] with him.

key_terms.عَافَاكُمُ اللَّهُ: May Allah grant you well-being (plural supplication)
key_terms.غَيْرُهُ: Others (referring to angels or unseen companions)

ai.seo_question: Why is the plural form used when addressing a single person in Islamic etiquette?
ai.summary: In Shia jurisprudence, this hadith from al-Kafi establishes the grammatical principle of 'plural for the single' (al-jama' li-l-wahid) in social etiquette, rooted in the belief that unseen entities like angels accompany the individual. It specifically applies to responses to sneezing, greetings, and supplications, emphasizing that the plural verb or pronoun acknowledges the presence of these spiritual witnesses alongside the person addressed.
